title: Joshua 6:22–27
context: Joshua 6:22–27 tells how the two spies keep their oath and bring Rahab’s family out before the city is burned. The narrator notes that she lives in Israel to this day. Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho, which 1 Kings 16:34 reports was fulfilled in the days of Ahab. The chapter closes by saying the LORD was with Joshua. Rahab’s rescue is largely shared ground: the New Testament commends her faith (Hebrews 11:31) and her works (James 2:25), and she appears in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:5).

verses.text: Joshua said to the two men who had spied out the land, “Go into the prostitute’s house, and bring the woman and all that she has out from there, as you swore to her.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua tells the two spies to bring Rahab and everything she has out of her house, as they swore to her. Arminians stress the binding force of an oath, even one made to a Canaanite, and see Israel’s faithfulness to its word as reflecting God’s own faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the promise made in Joshua 2:12–21 is kept exactly. Both traditions see the scarlet cord agreement fulfilled here and read the scene as God honoring Rahab’s faith through the faithfulness of his people.

verses.text: The young men who were spies went in, and brought out Rahab with her father, her mother, her brothers, and all that she had. They also brought out all of her relatives, and they set them outside of the camp of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The young spies bring out Rahab with her father, mother, brothers, and all her relatives, and set them outside the camp of Israel. Arminian readers see grace extending to her whole household because of her faith, and note that they first stay outside the camp before being joined to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that being placed outside the camp likely reflects the purity laws for those not yet part of the covenant people. Both traditions see her rescue extending to her family, as in other household rescues in Scripture, and read her later inclusion in Israel (6:25) as the completion.

verses.text: They burned the city with fire, and all that was in it. Only they put the silver, the gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron into the treasury of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel burns the city and everything in it, except the silver, gold, and vessels of bronze and iron, which go into the treasury of the LORD’s house. Arminians note the careful obedience here, in contrast with Achan in the next chapter, and see the burning as the completion of the herem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and observe that the phrase "the LORD’s house" is used here before there is a temple. Interpreters read it as the tabernacle or the sanctuary treasury. Both traditions read the verse as the full dedication of Jericho to the LORD.

verses.text: But Rahab the prostitute, her father’s household, and all that she had, Joshua saved alive. She lives in the middle of Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua saves alive Rahab and her father’s household, and she lives in Israel "to this day" because she hid the messengers. Arminian readers see a Gentile prostitute incorporated into Israel, showing that God’s mercy reaches outsiders who turn to him, and they note James 2:25 commends her action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Rahab as a sign of the grace that would later be extended to the nations, noting that Matthew 1:5 names her in the line of David and of Christ. Both traditions read "to this day" as indicating the account was written while her family was still known in Israel.

verses.text: Joshua commanded them with an oath at that time, saying, “Cursed is the man before the LORD who rises up and builds this city Jericho. With the loss of his firstborn he will lay its foundation, and with the loss of his youngest son he will set up its gates.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua pronounces a curse before the LORD on anyone who rebuilds Jericho: he will lose his firstborn at the foundation and his youngest at the gates. Arminians read the curse as preserving Jericho’s ruins as a lasting memorial of God’s judgment, and as a warning against undoing what God has done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that 1 Kings 16:34 records its fulfillment when Hiel rebuilt Jericho in Ahab’s day. Both traditions see the fulfillment as confirmation that the word spoken before the LORD does not fail, even centuries later.

verses.text: So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was in all the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread through the land. Arminians see God keeping his promise to be with Joshua as he was with Moses (Joshua 1:5), and see Joshua’s fame as the result of faithful obedience in the Jericho campaign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the verse credits Joshua’s success to the LORD’s presence. Both traditions read the chapter’s closing summary as the key to the whole account: Jericho fell because God was with his servant, not because of Joshua’s own strength.
